title: Yuxue Zhu
text: Hi! I’m a software developer currently pursuing the Master of Data Science (MDS) program at the University of British Columbia. With experience in full-stack and backend development, I’m expanding my skills in data analysis, statistics, and machine learning. I’m looking to transition my software engineering background into a career in data science or data engineering, where I can build data-driven solutions to solve real-world problems.

title: My first week in MDS
text:
My first few week in the MDS program have been both exciting and intense. Everything moves so quickly that sometimes it feels like I’ve accomplished a month’s worth of work in just one week! After being away from school for several years, coming back to the classroom has brought back a sense of excitement and energy for learning. Every day feels full, with new things to learn, new challenges to work through, and new experiences to enjoy.
I was getting familiar with all the different software, tools, and course schedules, while trying to keep up with the fast pace of the program. One of the best parts so far has been meeting so many new friends. Having people around who are going through the same experience makes the busy days feel more enjoyable.
Although the first few week have been challenging, it has also been very fulfilling. I am gradually finding my rhythm, getting better at managing my time, and becoming more comfortable with the new tools and concepts.

title: Penguins Analysis with R
text:
Introduction
In this post, I explore the palmerpenguins dataset using R. I focus on penguin species, body mass, and flipper length.
Data source: palmerpenguins


Setup
Load the packages needed for the analysis. I suppress messages and warnings so that the rendered page focuses on the analysis.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)



Exploring the data
First, check the structure of dataset.

head(penguins)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA          NA
5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>


The dataset contains 344 observations and 8 variables.
Next, calculate the number of penguins and average body mass for each species.

species_summary <- penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_body_mass_g = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

species_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species       n mean_body_mass_g sd_body_mass_g
  <fct>     <int>            <dbl>          <dbl>
1 Adelie      152            3701.           459.
2 Chinstrap    68            3733.           384.
3 Gentoo      124            5076.           504.


The summary shows differences in body mass among the three species. Gentoo penguins have the highest average body mass, while Adelie penguins have the lowest.


Visualizing body mass
Create a boxplot to compare body mass across species.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Species",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    title = "Penguin Body Mass by Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).








Figure 1: Body mass of penguins by species.





The figure shows that Gentoo penguins generally have greater body mass than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.


Flipper length and body mass
Calculate the correlation between flipper length and body mass.

cor(
  penguins$flipper_length_mm,
  penguins$body_mass_g,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

[1] 0.8712018


The positive correlation indicates that penguins with longer flippers tend to have greater body mass.


Conclusion
The analysis shows differences in body mass among penguin species. Gentoo penguins generally have the greatest body mass, and penguins with longer flippers tend to be heavier.

title: Penguins Analysis with R and Python
text:
Introduction
This post demonstrates how R and Python can be used together in the same Quarto document.Use the reticulate package to pass objects between R and Python.
Data source: Palmer Penguins


Setup

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(reticulate)



Calculate a result in R

species_mass <- penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
  species_mass

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   mean_body_mass_g
  <fct>                <dbl>
1 Adelie               3701.
2 Chinstrap            3733.
3 Gentoo               5076.




Use the R object in Python

species_mass_summary = r.species_mass
print(species_mass_summary)

     species  mean_body_mass_g
0     Adelie       3700.662252
1  Chinstrap       3733.088235
2     Gentoo       5076.016260

mean_mass = species_mass_summary["mean_body_mass_g"].mean()
print(f"Mean body mass: {mean_mass:.2f} g")

Mean body mass: 4169.92 g




Use the python object in R

mean_mass_from_python <- py$mean_mass

mean_mass_from_python

[1] 4169.922
